stem: An associate uploads a 40-page quarterly operations report and types 'Summarise this report'. Claude returns three generic paragraphs that never mention the cost overruns the CFO wants to see. What is the most likely cause of the poor output?

options.text: The prompt gave no audience, purpose or required content, so Claude produced a general-purpose summary.
options.why: Without knowing who the summary is for and what must be covered, the model defaults to a broad overview; the fix is to specify the CFO audience, the cost focus, length and format.

options.text: The report is too long for Claude to read, so it summarised only the introduction.
options.why: A 40-page document is well within what Claude can read in one conversation; the summary is generic because the request was, not because the file was truncated.

options.text: The model is underperforming today and the associate should try a different AI platform.
options.why: Generic output from a generic prompt is expected behaviour, not a platform fault; switching tools without fixing the prompt reproduces the problem.

options.text: Claude cannot summarise financial content reliably unless the figures are provided as a spreadsheet rather than embedded in a PDF.
options.why: Claude can summarise financial narrative in a document; the file format is not the issue here.

explanation: The first diagnosis for a vague or generic output is a vague prompt. Stating the audience, the purpose, what must be included and the desired length and format gives the model what it needs to produce a targeted summary.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices (be clear and direct, add context)

stem: A marketing team shares a 'campaign brief generator' prompt that reads: 'Write a compelling, creative campaign brief for our new product. Make it specific and engaging.' Across six products the briefs come back nearly identical, with placeholder-style claims and no product detail. Which change would most directly fix the problem?

options.text: Add the product's features, audience, positioning and tone to each run, and include one or two examples of briefs the team rates highly.
options.why: Generic output is diagnosed as missing context and missing examples; providing both gives Claude the raw material and the standard to match.

options.text: Add 'You MUST be highly specific, original and detailed. Do NOT write generic content' in capitals at the top of the prompt and repeat it at the end.
options.why: Stronger adjectives do not supply the missing information; the model still has nothing product-specific to work from.

options.text: Switch the team to the most capable model so it can infer the product details.
options.why: No model can infer facts about an unreleased product that are absent from the prompt; capability is not the constraint.

options.text: Ask Claude to write the brief three times and pick the longest version.
options.why: Longer generic output is still generic; volume does not address the missing inputs.

explanation: When a shared prompt returns the same generic answer for different inputs, the diagnosis is almost always missing context and missing examples. Vague quality adjectives and bigger models do not substitute for specific inputs and a concrete example of good.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices (add context, use examples)

stem: A sales enablement Project answers reps' questions about pricing. For the last three weeks it has quoted the old price list, even though the pricing team published a new one. The Project's knowledge contains a PDF named 'Price list 2025 Q1' and the instructions say 'Always use the price list in Project knowledge'. What is the diagnosis and fix?

options.text: The instructions are too weak; rewrite them to say 'Use ONLY the latest prices' so Claude looks up the current list.
options.why: Claude cannot reach a newer price list that is not in its knowledge; instruction wording does not change what data is available.

options.text: The model has memorised old prices from training; switching models will fix it.
options.why: The answers match the outdated file in the Project, which is the actual source; changing models would still read the same stale document.

options.text: Reps should start each chat by pasting the new prices, since Project knowledge cannot be changed.
options.why: Project knowledge can be updated; pushing the fix onto every rep in every chat is error-prone and defeats the purpose of the Project.

options.text: The Project knowledge is stale: replace the old PDF with the current price list and remove the superseded file.
options.why: The Project is doing exactly what it was configured to do with the data it has; updating the knowledge source resolves the outdated answers.

explanation: When a Project gives outdated answers consistently, check the knowledge sources before touching the instructions or model. Stale documents produce stale, confident answers, and the fix is to replace and remove superseded files.
reference: Claude Help Center — Projects (managing project knowledge)

stem: A product manager has been working with Claude in a single conversation for two days on a launch plan; it is now about 80 turns long. Recently Claude has contradicted decisions agreed earlier and forgotten the agreed audience. The most recent message asked it to revise the timeline, rewrite the FAQ, draft three emails, build a risk register and propose pricing in one go, and the response was shallow on all five. Which two actions most directly address the problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Start a fresh conversation that opens with a concise summary of the decisions made so far and the agreed audience.
options.why: A very long conversation degrades focus and eventually hits the length limit; restarting with a written summary restores a clean, complete context.

options.text: Add 'Remember everything we agreed above' to the next message.
options.why: The problem is the volume and dilution of context, which an instruction cannot undo.

options.text: Split the five-part request into separate, sequenced requests, checking each result before moving on.
options.why: An overloaded request spreads attention thinly; one task at a time gives each the depth it needs and makes errors easy to spot.

options.text: Move to a higher plan tier to get a larger usage limit so the conversation can continue.
options.why: Usage limits govern how much you can use Claude overall; they are unrelated to the quality loss in one overlong conversation.

options.text: Resend the same five-part message but ask for a much longer answer.
options.why: A longer answer to an overloaded request in a bloated context will be longer, not better.

explanation: Two separate faults are present: an overlong conversation whose context has become diluted, and an overloaded request. The remedies are to restart with a summary of what matters and to break the request into sequential pieces. Instructions to remember, plan upgrades and longer outputs do not treat either cause.
reference: Claude Help Center — How do usage and length limits work?; Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices

stem: A compliance team's Project has instructions that say 'Answer in British English and cite the section of the policy document you relied on'. Most chats behave correctly. One colleague reports that her answers use US spelling and never cite sections. Looking at her screen, you see she started the chat from the main chat page and attached the policy document manually. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: The instructions are not forceful enough and should be rewritten with 'MUST' and repeated at the end.
options.why: The same instructions work for everyone else; their wording is not the variable that differs in this case.

options.text: The attached policy document was long enough to push the Project instructions out of the context window, so they were silently dropped for that chat.
options.why: Project instructions are not displaced by an attachment; besides, the chat was never inside the Project.

options.text: The chat was started outside the Project, so its instructions and knowledge never applied; she should start the chat inside the Project.
options.why: Project instructions apply only to conversations created within that Project; a chat from the main page with a manual attachment has none of the Project's configuration.

options.text: The model was switched to a different one that ignores custom instructions.
options.why: All the available models follow Project instructions; the difference here is where the chat lives, not which model answered.

explanation: Diagnosing a configuration problem means checking what actually applied to the conversation. Project instructions and knowledge only take effect in chats started inside the Project, so a chat begun elsewhere will behave as if the configuration did not exist, regardless of instruction wording or model.
reference: Claude Help Center — Projects (how project instructions apply)

stem: An associate asks Claude to draft an email reminding 200 volunteers about Saturday's event. The draft is accurate but reads like a legal notice. What is the best next step?

options.text: Send the draft anyway, since the facts are right and tone is secondary.
options.why: Tone determines whether volunteers read and act on the message; accepting an ill-suited draft wastes the chance to fix it in one turn.

options.text: Start a new chat and type the original request again, since a fresh conversation usually produces a different and possibly warmer draft.
options.why: Repeating an identical request discards the useful draft and gives Claude no information about what to change.

options.text: Ask Claude to explain why its draft sounds formal.
options.why: An explanation does not produce a better email; the productive move is to give a concrete revision instruction.

options.text: Reply with specific feedback: keep the date, time and place, make it friendly, and cut it to two short paragraphs.
options.why: Iterating on the existing draft with precise feedback about what to keep and what to change is the fastest route to the result.

explanation: Adjusting based on results means giving Claude specific, actionable feedback on the draft it produced, naming what to keep and what to change, rather than accepting a poor fit or starting from scratch.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices (iterate and refine)

stem: A customer-success lead added two example responses to her prompt for drafting replies to cancellation requests, and quality improved. But now every reply follows the examples' exact three-paragraph structure and offers the same 10% retention discount, even for customers whose situation does not call for it. How should she adjust?

options.text: Remove both examples, since they are clearly causing the problem.
options.why: The examples raised quality; removing them returns the prompt to the state that produced weaker replies.

options.text: Replace the two similar examples with a varied set covering different cancellation reasons, and state that they show tone rather than a fixed offer.
options.why: Over-fitting to examples is corrected by diversifying them and by saying explicitly what they are meant to illustrate.

options.text: Add three more examples that also offer the 10% discount so the pattern is reinforced and the replies become even more consistent across customers.
options.why: More examples of the same pattern will make the over-copying worse, not better.

options.text: Tell Claude to be more creative with each reply.
options.why: A vague adjective does not tell the model which aspects of the examples to vary and which to keep.

explanation: Examples are powerful but the model copies what it sees. When outputs become too uniform, adjust by making the example set diverse and by stating what the examples illustrate, rather than dropping examples or adding vague instructions.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Use examples (multishot prompting)

stem: An operations analyst asks Claude in one message to clean a pasted data extract, calculate monthly averages, write a narrative on the trends and lay out slide content. The narrative reads well, but two of the monthly averages are wrong and the slides repeat the errors. What adjustment should she make?

options.text: Break the work into steps: clean the data, then calculate and verify the averages, and only then ask for the narrative and slides.
options.why: Splitting an overloaded request lets each step be checked, and stops errors in the numbers from propagating into everything built on them.

options.text: Resend the same message with 'double-check all calculations and show your working before writing the narrative' added at the end.
options.why: A self-check instruction inside an overloaded request is unreliable, and any remaining errors still flow straight into the narrative and slides.

options.text: Ask Claude to regenerate the slides only, since the narrative is fine.
options.why: The slides repeat wrong averages; regenerating downstream content without fixing the numbers reproduces the errors.

options.text: Switch to a faster model so she can rerun the request several times and compare.
options.why: Rerunning an overloaded request is a lottery; the structural fix is to sequence and verify, not to sample faster.

explanation: When a multi-part request produces errors in an early step that contaminate later steps, adjust by decomposing the work and inserting a verification point after the step that matters most, so later outputs build on checked results.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices (break complex tasks into steps)

stem: A market analyst asks Claude in a normal chat 'What are the current pricing tiers of our three main competitors?' The answer is fluent but has no sources, and one competitor changed its pricing last month, which the answer does not reflect. She has already rephrased the question twice with the same result. What is the right adjustment?

options.text: Switch to the most capable model and ask again, since it reasons more carefully.
options.why: A more capable model without access to the web still has no way to know about a pricing change made last month; reasoning power is not the gap.

options.text: Add 'Use only the most up-to-date information available' to the prompt.
options.why: An instruction cannot give the model information it does not have; it will answer from training knowledge regardless.

options.text: Provide two examples of well-formatted competitor comparisons, each with a sources column, so the answer follows the same layout.
options.why: Examples shape format; they cannot make the underlying facts current or produce genuine citations.

options.text: Run the question with web search or research mode enabled so Claude retrieves and cites current pages.
options.why: The failure is about currency and sourcing, which needs live retrieval; the right adjustment is a different capability, not a third rephrasing.

explanation: Adjusting based on results includes recognising when the prompt is not the problem. Questions that need current, cited facts require a feature that retrieves them, such as web search or research mode; rephrasing, bigger models and examples cannot supply information the model does not have.
reference: Claude Help Center — Web search and Research in Claude

stem: A legal-operations team has revised its contract-summary prompt six times over two weeks. Each revision fixed the most recent complaint and caused a new one: shortening the summary dropped the termination clause, adding the clause made summaries too long, and so on. Each reviewer tests the prompt on whichever contract is on their desk. Which two changes to how the team iterates would most improve results? (Choose two.)

options.text: Write down explicit success criteria first, such as the required clauses and a maximum length, and test every version against the same set of five representative contracts.
options.why: Fixed criteria and a fixed test set turn iteration into measurement, so a change that fixes one thing and breaks another is caught before it ships.

options.text: Switch to a different model at each iteration so that model behaviour is not the bottleneck.
options.why: Changing the model at the same time as the prompt makes it impossible to tell which change caused which effect.

options.text: Ask Claude to rate each summary out of 10 and keep the prompt version with the highest average.
options.why: Self-ratings are not a reliable measure of accuracy or completeness; the team's own criteria and review are.

options.text: Change one element of the prompt per iteration and keep a version log recording what changed and what the test results were.
options.why: Isolating changes and logging outcomes shows which edits help, which regress, and lets the team return to a known-good version.

options.text: Let each reviewer keep a personal copy of the prompt and tune it to their own preferences.
options.why: Diverging copies multiply the inconsistency and remove any shared standard for what a good summary is.

explanation: Effective iteration is disciplined: define what good looks like before changing anything, test each version on the same representative inputs, change one thing at a time and record results. Without that, each fix simply trades one failure for another.
reference: Claude Platform docs — Prompting best practices (define success criteria, iterate systematically)

stem: Every week an internal-communications associate starts a new chat, pastes the same 600-word style guide and tone rules, and then asks Claude to draft the staff newsletter. What is the most effective way to streamline this?

options.text: Keep one very long conversation open for the whole year so the style guide only needs pasting once and Claude keeps all the context.
options.why: A never-ending conversation eventually degrades and hits the length limit; it is a fragile way to persist instructions.

options.text: Create a Project with the style guide and tone rules in its instructions and knowledge, and start each week's chat there.
options.why: Projects persist instructions and reference material across conversations, which is exactly what recurring work needs.

options.text: Ask Claude at the start of each chat to remember the style guide from last week.
options.why: A new chat has no access to previous chats' content unless a feature such as Projects or memory supplies it.

options.text: Shorten the style guide to 100 words so pasting it is quicker.
options.why: Cutting guidance to save typing loses the detail that makes drafts consistent; the pasting itself is the inefficiency to remove.

explanation: Recurring work with stable instructions and reference material belongs in a Project. It removes repetitive setup, keeps every chat consistent, and makes updates a single change rather than a weekly copy-paste.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects?

stem: Eight agents on a support team each write their own prompts to draft replies to warranty claims. Quality varies widely: some replies omit the claim number, others use a different tone, and the team lead spends an hour a day correcting them. Which optimisation best addresses the inconsistency?

options.text: Require all agents to use the most capable model available so their individual prompts produce better drafts without further changes.
options.why: Eight different prompts on a better model are still eight different prompts; the variation comes from the inputs, not the model.

options.text: Have the team lead write every reply personally to guarantee consistency.
options.why: This removes the productivity gain entirely and makes the lead the bottleneck.

options.text: Build a shared Project holding the reply template, tone rules and two example replies, with a standard prompt for claim details.
options.why: A shared configuration and template standardise the inputs, so drafts are consistent and the lead's corrections drop.

options.text: Ask each agent to add 'be consistent with the team style' to their personal prompts.
options.why: Claude cannot see the team style from that phrase; consistency comes from shared, explicit instructions and examples.

explanation: When several people do the same task with Claude, inconsistency is usually a symptom of unshared prompts. Centralising the template, rules and examples in a shared Project with a standard prompt is the optimisation that fixes quality and saves review time.
reference: Claude Help Center — Projects (sharing projects with your team)

stem: A finance team uses Claude to draft a weekly performance report that goes to 30 clients. The workflow is: paste the data, generate the report, send. Twice this quarter a wrong percentage reached clients. The team wants to keep the time savings but stop the errors. Which change best fits?

options.text: Add 'double-check every figure before answering' to the prompt.
options.why: A self-check instruction is a weak safeguard; the model can restate a wrong figure confidently, and nothing outside the model catches it.

options.text: Go back to writing the reports by hand to eliminate the risk.
options.why: This discards the workflow gains; a review checkpoint achieves the reliability at far lower cost.

options.text: Generate the report twice with slightly different prompts and send whichever version looks more polished and internally consistent.
options.why: Polish is not accuracy, and neither version has been checked against the source data.

options.text: Add a review checkpoint before sending: a team member checks each figure against the source data using a short checklist.
options.why: A human verification step placed between generation and sending catches errors where they are cheap to fix and preserves the rest of the time savings.

explanation: Optimising a workflow is not only about speed. Placing a lightweight human review checkpoint at the point of highest consequence, with a checklist that focuses on the things that have gone wrong before, keeps the efficiency while making the output trustworthy.
reference: Responsible-AI practice — human review checkpoints in AI-assisted workflows

stem: An operations manager reviews 12 vendors every month. For each vendor she opens a new chat, describes the scoring rubric from memory, pastes the vendor's performance data and asks for a written assessment; the whole job takes two days. Which two changes would most improve efficiency without lowering the quality of the assessments? (Choose two.)

options.text: Put the scoring rubric and the assessment template into a Project's instructions and knowledge so every vendor is assessed against the same standard.
options.why: Persisting the rubric removes the repeated explanation and eliminates drift between vendors.

options.text: Run all 12 vendors through one long conversation so Claude can compare them as it goes.
options.why: One very long conversation dilutes context and risks the length limit; it slows each assessment and mixes vendors' data.

options.text: Use a saved prompt that takes a vendor's data file and returns the assessment in a fixed format, then spend her review time on vendors whose scores changed or fell below threshold.
options.why: A standard prompt with a fixed output format makes each run fast and comparable, and directing review to exceptions keeps quality where it matters.

options.text: Skip reviewing assessments for vendors that scored well last month.
options.why: Last month's score is not evidence about this month; unreviewed assessments can miss a decline.

options.text: Have Claude email each vendor its assessment directly to remove the manager from the loop.
options.why: Removing the human from an external communication with commercial consequences trades a small time saving for a large risk.

explanation: Recurring, repetitive work is optimised by persisting stable context in a Project, standardising the prompt and output format, and focusing human review on exceptions. Long single conversations and dropping review are false economies.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects?; Usage limit best practices

stem: A policy team's Project has grown over a year to 40 knowledge files, including several superseded versions of the same procedures. Users report that answers have become slower, that Claude sometimes cites a withdrawn procedure, and that they hit their usage limits sooner than in other Projects. Which single optimisation best addresses all three complaints?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to ignore any file whose title contains an old year or the word 'superseded', and to cite only current files.
options.why: The superseded files still occupy the Project's context, so speed and usage do not improve, and an instruction is an unreliable way to stop citations of old content.

options.text: Prune the knowledge: remove superseded files, keep only current procedures, and add a short index stating which file is authoritative.
options.why: Removing stale material reduces what is loaded with each chat, which addresses speed and usage, and eliminates the withdrawn procedures that were being cited.

options.text: Ask users to upgrade their plan so the extra usage does not matter.
options.why: A bigger allowance does not fix wrong citations or slowness, and it pays for waste rather than removing it.

options.text: Ask Claude in a chat to delete the outdated files from the Project.
options.why: Claude cannot modify Project knowledge from within a conversation; a person must curate the files.

explanation: Project knowledge is part of what Claude works with in every chat, so a bloated, outdated knowledge base costs speed and usage and produces stale answers. Curating the files, removing superseded versions and adding an index is the optimisation that fixes all three symptoms at once.
reference: Claude Help Center — Projects (managing project knowledge); Usage limit best practices
